title: 24 Hours on a Night Shift as a Cardiac Step-Down Nurse
creator: Maria Santos RN
description:
A full 12-hour night shift with me (no patients filmed, obviously).

Thanks to Huel for sponsoring! Get 15% off + a free shaker with code MARIA at https://huel.com/maria

Compression socks, stethoscope, bag: I get asked a lot, I'll do a separate video.

My sleep routine after nights: https://youtube.com/watch?v=mariasleep1

sentences.t: It's six forty p.m., and I'm getting ready for a twelve-hour night shift on a cardiac step-down unit.
I've been a nurse for six years, on nights for four of them, and a lot of you asked what a shift actually looks like.
So I'm bringing you along, minus anything with patients in it, obviously.
First, the bag.
Compression socks are already on, because twelve hours on your feet without them is how you end up with legs like tree trunks.
In the bag, a spare set of scrubs, my stethoscope, three pens because they will get stolen, and a phone charger with an extra-long cable.
And food, because the cafeteria closes at eight and the vending machine is a war crime.
Seven p.m., I'm on the unit, and we start with handoff.
The day nurse walks me through each of my patients, what happened today, their meds, and anything to watch for overnight.
I have four patients tonight, which is a normal load for this unit.
The first couple of hours are busy, evening meds, assessments, getting everyone settled for the night.
Around ten, one of my patients' heart rhythm changes on the monitor, so I loop in the doctor, and we adjust a medication.
That's a pretty typical night, honestly, lots of small things, and you're always watching the monitors out of the corner of your eye.
Two a.m. is my break.
This is the part of the night where your body is very clearly asking you what you think you're doing.
And that's actually where today's sponsor comes in, because this video is sponsored by Fuel.
For a long time my two a.m. meal was crackers and a granola bar from the vending machine, and I'd crash an hour later.
Now I bring a bottle of Fuel Black Edition, which is a complete meal in a shake, with forty grams of protein and all your vitamins and minerals.
It takes about ten seconds to make, and I can drink it at the nurses' station while I'm charting.
The chocolate one tastes like a milkshake, and it actually keeps me full until the end of the shift.
If your schedule is chaotic too, go to fuel dot com slash maria and use code MARIA for fifteen percent off, plus a free shaker with your first order.
So, back to the floor.
Three to five a.m. is the quiet zone, if you're lucky.
I use it to catch up on charting, restock my rooms, and check on everyone every hour.
This is also when people tend to wake up confused, so a lot of my job at four a.m. is sitting with someone and reminding them where they are.
Five thirty, morning labs get drawn, and then morning meds.
Seven a.m., handoff again, and this time I'm the one giving report.
And then I go home, and the sun is up, and every bird in the neighborhood is screaming at me.
Blackout curtains, white noise, phone on do not disturb, and I'm asleep by eight thirty.
I'll be up around three in the afternoon to do it all again tomorrow night.
If you're a nurse, or thinking about becoming one, ask me anything in the comments, I read all of them.
And if you're on nights tonight, drink some water, I see you.
